meta.title: Who really said "The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Ted Williams probably said it — but the wording survives only in a 2007 SABR interview with his pitcher Bob Humphreys. No contemporaneous source: attributed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers'?
meta.ogDescription: The wording rests on one 2007 SABR interview with Senators pitcher Bob Humphreys. No contemporaneous source. Attributed to Ted Williams, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Red Sox left fielder; Senators manager, 1969–1971
answer.sourceLine: The credit is plausible and the line is documented — but only as one man’s memory. Washington Senators pitcher Bob Humphreys recalled his manager saying it, in an interview given on 6 June 2007 and printed in the Society for American Baseball Research’s The National Pastime in 2009. No contemporaneous report of the remark has surfaced, and a different phrasing of the same joke appears in Ben Bradlee Jr.’s Williams biography, so the polished sentence everyone quotes cannot be pinned to a primary source.

docMeta.dd: Ted Williams, as recalled by pitcher Bob Humphreys
Author’s interview with Bob Humphreys, 6 June 2007 (note 6)

source.excerpt: I had no problems with him. I would rag on him and he would give it right back. He would say, ‘The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers.’
source.trailTitle: How the line got to you
trail: 1969 — Williams takes over the expansion Washington Senators, goes 86–76 in the club’s only winning season in Washington, and is named Manager of the Year. He manages the franchise through 1972. Wikipedia ↗

6 June 2007 — Steve Walker interviews Bob Humphreys, who pitched for the Senators from April 1966 until his release in June 1970, for a piece on Williams’s first Washington team. Humphreys’s SABR biography ↗
2009 — the line reaches print, inside Humphreys’s recollection, in SABR’s convention journal. This is the earliest printing we were able to locate. The National Pastime: Monumental Baseball ↗
2013 — a different phrasing of the same joke appears in Ben Bradlee Jr.’s biography The Kid: The Immortal Life of Ted Williams, put as a question and answer. Internet Archive full-text search ↗
source.excerptNote: The speaker here is Humphreys, quoting Williams. The words attributed to Williams are inside his pitcher’s recollection, given in a 2007 interview — not a transcript, a recording or a report made at the time.

source.rightsHolder: Society for American Baseball Research and Steve Walker (The National Pastime, 2009); the remark itself is attributed to Ted Williams and his estate
source.rightsNote: The remark was spoken, not published, so rights attach to the work that carries it — Steve Walker’s article in The National Pastime: Monumental Baseball, published by SABR in 2009 and still in copyright. Ben Bradlee Jr.’s The Kid (Little, Brown, 2013), which records the other phrasing, is likewise in copyright. Because no pre-1931 publication of this line exists, nothing here is in the public domain; quote the sentence with attribution rather than reproducing the surrounding passages.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.kicker: The hitter who never forgave the other guy
author.heading: Who was Ted Williams?
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder; manager, Washington Senators 1969–1971
author.bio: Ted Williams spent nineteen seasons with the Boston Red Sox, interrupted twice by military service, and finished with a .344 career batting average, 521 home runs and the highest on-base percentage in the history of the game. In 1941 he hit .406 — still the last time any major leaguer batted over .400 across a full season. He came back to the field as a manager in 1969, taking the expansion Washington Senators to 86–76 and Manager of the Year honours, and brought with him the one prejudice nineteen years in the batter’s box had hardened: a deep, cheerful, unshakeable low opinion of pitchers.

misattribution.heading: Not the wrong man — the wrong kind of certainty
misattribution.intro: This is not a stolen-quote case. No rival claimant exists, and every printing we found credits Williams. What the internet gets wrong is the confidence: the line is passed around as a documented Williams saying when it is an undated clubhouse memory, and the crisp sentence people quote is only one of two recorded phrasings.

items.who: Two different versions are in print
items.why: Humphreys’s recollection gives the polished declarative form. Ben Bradlee Jr.’s Williams biography The Kid gives it as a set-up and punchline instead — “What do you think is dumber than a pitcher? Two pitchers.” — in a passage that runs straight on into Senators pitcher Dick Bosman’s further recollections. Compare the snippets ↗

Sites such as Quotes.net list the sentence under Williams’s name with no source, no date and no context, sitting next to other unsourced Williams lines. That is where most people meet it. Quotes.net ↗

Wikiquote’s Ted Williams article does not carry the line at all. It sits on the article’s talk page, under a heading that reads simply “Unsourced” — the holding pen for quotes nobody has been able to cite. Talk:Ted Williams ↗

Williams managed in Washington from 1969; Humphreys described the exchange to Steve Walker in an interview dated 6 June 2007, and it reached print two years after that. We found no newspaper, broadcast or book record of the line from the years it was supposedly said. The interview note ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Williams almost certainly said something very like this — the joke turns up in more than one book about him, in more than one form, always from the men who pitched for him. What nobody has produced is a record made at the time. The exact sentence quoted everywhere is a single pitcher’s memory, given in 2007 and printed in 2009. Read the passage ↗

context.heading: Why a hitter would say this
lead: Williams spent nineteen seasons trying to beat pitchers and then, in 1969, found himself managing a clubhouse full of them. His first Washington team went 86–76 — the only winning season the franchise ever had in Washington — and he was named Manager of the Year for it, so nobody much minded the ribbing. Wikipedia’s account of his managing years ↗

The line survives because it was part of a running argument. Humphreys told Steve Walker that he would rag Williams and Williams would give it right back — the pitcher countering that he would like a job where you could fail six times out of ten and still be a star, and Williams answering that with the right stuff to throw at, he might have hit .600. That exchange, not a lectern or a book, is the natural home of the line. Read the passage at SABR ↗
context.detailsSummary: What would move this from ‘attributed’ to ‘verified’?
detailsBody: A contemporaneous record — a 1969–71 newspaper column, wire story or broadcast transcript in which a reporter quotes Williams saying it at the time, rather than a player remembering it decades afterwards.

Or Williams’s own words in print. The remark appears in neither of the books he wrote with John Underwood, and a full-text search of the Internet Archive’s digitised book corpus returns the exact sentence “the only thing dumber than a pitcher…” in no book at all. See the search ↗
Until then the honest verdict is the one on this page: he very likely said it, in some form, and the form you see quoted is a single pitcher’s memory of how it went.
context.pull: “I would rag on him and he would give it right back.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Steve Walker's SABR article quotes Bob Humphreys saying Williams would tell him "The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers," footnoted (note 6) to the author's interview with Bob Humphreys, 6 June 2007; the article was published in The National Pastime: Monumental Baseball (Washington, DC, 2009).
Wikiquote's Ted Williams article does NOT contain the line; its only section headings are 'Quotes', 'Quotes about Ted Williams' and 'External links'.

The Talk:Ted Williams page carries the line under a section headed 'Unsourced', alongside other uncited Williams quotations including 'Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer.'

A full-text search of the Internet Archive book corpus for "dumber than a pitcher" returns five hits; Ben Bradlee Jr.'s The Kid: The Immortal Life of Ted Williams renders the joke as "What do you think is dumber than a pitcher? Two pitchers." The exact string "only thing dumber than a pitcher" returns zero hits.
Bob Humphreys was traded to the Washington Senators on 2 April 1966 and remained with the club until Washington released him on 13 June 1970, covering Williams's first season as manager.

Ted Williams lived 30 August 1918 – 5 July 2002, batted .406 in 1941 and is the last major leaguer to bat over .400 in a season, finished with a .344 career average, and managed the Washington Senators from 1969 to 1971 (86–76 and Manager of the Year in 1969) before continuing with the Texas Rangers.
Quotes.net lists 'The only thing dumber than a pitcher is two pitchers.' under Ted Williams's name with no source or citation.
